case_analysis.focal_point: Whether oil companies can remove Louisiana coastal-damage tort suits to federal court under the federal-officer removal statute based on their World War II-era federal refining/supply contracts, on the theory that the suits “relate to” acts done “under” federal direction.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1442(a)(1) (federal-officer removal statute), including its 2011 amendment expanding removability to actions “for or relating to any act under color of [federal] office.”
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Chevron and others) argue that removal is proper because, during World War II, they performed critical crude-oil production/refining activities under close federal direction via wartime contracting and coordination (e.g., aviation gasoline procurement), and the parishes’ alleged coastal harm is sufficiently connected to those federally directed operations. Relying on the statute’s broadened “for or relating to” language (especially after the 2011 amendment) and the policy of protecting federal operations from state-court interference, petitioners contend that the required nexus is satisfied at least where the asserted injuries would not have occurred but for (or are factually intertwined with) federally directed wartime production and refining. They also press that a broad construction avoids chilling private cooperation with federal emergency mobilization and ensures a neutral federal forum where federal defenses can be adjudicated.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the parishes and Louisiana) argue removal is improper because their complaints target decades of coastal land-loss and wetlands damage from oil-and-gas extraction, waste disposal, canal dredging, and related conduct that would have occurred regardless of any discrete WWII aviation-gasoline refining contracts. They contend petitioners’ theory stretches “relating to” into an unlimited but-for chain (e.g., because crude oil is an input to wartime refining, any upstream conduct becomes removable), collapsing the statute’s limits and contradicting Watson’s requirement that a private actor must be assisting or carrying out a federal officer’s delegated task—not merely operating in a heavily regulated or war-influenced industry. Respondents also emphasize factual and legal mismatches: the suits do not challenge wartime refining performance, and the alleged marsh-damaging practices were largely civilian-market driven and not directed by federal officers. They additionally argue petitioners forfeited or abandoned certain nexus theories below (a point the United States disputes only in part in the excerpts), and that accepting petitioners’ approach would federalize large swaths of state tort law whenever defendants can identify some historic federal contract in their corporate past.
key_precedents: Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., 551 U.S. 142 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that Congress in 2011 added “or relating to,” and as Justice Gorsuch notes that amendment must expand the nexus beyond a strict causal-connection test. But that expansion cannot be read to swallow Watson’s independent “acting under” requirement, which still demands delegation-like assistance to a federal superior tied to the conduct the plaintiff challenges—not merely participation in an upstream market influenced by wartime procurement. Justice Kagan’s line-drawing concern persuades me that accepting a crude-to-avgas but-for chain here would effectively convert § 1442 into a historical-contract removal statute with no workable limiting principle, undermining institutional legitimacy and the federal-state balance. A narrow holding—assuming arguendo some qualifying wartime contracts—can still reject removal because the complaints target decades of dredging, disposal, and extraction practices not shown to have been federally directed or undertaken “under color” of federal office.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest textual point is the 2011 addition of “or relating to,” but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, that amendment expands only the nexus element; it does not displace § 1442’s separate, antecedent requirement that the defendant be “acting under” a federal officer in the sense Watson describes—assisting with a delegated federal task. Even crediting wartime procurement as a federal program, the parishes’ complaints target dredging, disposal, and extraction practices not alleged to have been directed by federal officers, so the asserted crude-to-avgas connection is an attenuated but-for chain that fails to satisfy “act under color of such office” in the statutory text. Under an original public meaning approach, reading “relating to” to reach any upstream historical supply activity would effectively erase these limiting words and transform § 1442 into a general contracting-based removal statute without clear congressional command. No colleague identified precedent undermining Watson’s constraint, so my view remains that removal is improper on this record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains the 2011 addition of “or relating to” and Congress’s instruction to construe § 1442 liberally, but that cannot be read to dissolve the statute’s independent limits. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, Watson’s “acting under” requirement demands a delegation/assistance relationship tied to the conduct the plaintiff is suing about, and an attenuated crude-to-avgas supply-chain story does not show federal direction over the marsh-damaging dredging, disposal, and extraction practices alleged here. Interpreting “relating to” to reach any upstream activity historically connected to federal procurement would effectively federalize routine state tort litigation whenever a defendant once supplied the Government—an overbroad practical consequence with no clear textual stopping point. On this record, the nexus is too remote and the pleaded claims do not seek to impose liability for performance of any federally directed task, so removal fails.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains that Congress’s 2011 “for or relating to” amendment broadens the nexus and § 1442 is to be liberally construed, but that does not eliminate Watson’s threshold requirement that the private party be genuinely “acting under” federal direction in the conduct the suit challenges. Chief Justice Roberts’s line-drawing concern is decisive for me: accepting an attenuated crude-to-avgas-to-coastal-operations chain would make “relating to” functionally boundless and federalize ordinary state tort claims without a clear limiting principle. Justice Kagan is also right that the complaints, as pleaded, target decades of dredging, disposal, and extraction practices not shown to have been directed by a federal officer, so even a relaxed nexus fails because it is untethered from an “act under color of” federal office. Given the practical stakes for vulnerable coastal communities’ access to state-law remedies, I see no textual or precedential basis to stretch § 1442 beyond Watson’s constraint here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioners’ best textual point remains the 2011 amendment adding “or relating to,” which does broaden the nexus beyond a strict causation test, but it still cannot be read to swallow § 1442’s other limiting words. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Watson’s “acting under” requirement demands delegation-like assistance to a federal superior in carrying out a federal task, not merely operating in an industry important to wartime procurement; nothing in the record ties the parishes’ dredging, disposal, and extraction practices to federal direction in performing WWII obligations. Even under a liberal construction, accepting petitioners’ crude-to-avgas chain would turn “relating to” into an unbounded but-for hook that would federalize ordinary state tort suits whenever a defendant once supplied the Government, a result hard to square with the statute’s targeted protective purpose. No colleague identified a precedent that compels that breadth, so removal remains improper on this pleading and evidentiary posture.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest argument is that Congress in 2011 broadened § 1442(a)(1) to cover actions “for or relating to” federal office, so an upstream supply relationship to wartime avgas procurement should suffice. But as Chief Justice Roberts rightly stresses, liberal construction is “not limitless,” and Watson’s independent “acting under” requirement still demands a delegation-like relationship tied to the conduct the plaintiff is suing about, not merely participation in a federally important industry decades earlier. Even crediting the Fifth Circuit’s more relaxed nexus framing after the amendment, petitioners’ crude-to-avgas chain is too attenuated from the pleaded dredging, disposal, and extraction practices to give operative meaning to the statute’s limiting words (“acting under” and “under color of such office”). Accepting petitioners’ theory would effectively transform § 1442 into a general historical-procurement removal device without clear textual warrant, contrary to separation-of-powers and federalism baselines.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains that Congress’s 2011 addition of “or relating to” broadens the nexus requirement, but that amendment cannot be read to nullify Watson’s independent “acting under” threshold or to authorize an unbounded but-for chain. Chief Justice Roberts’s line-drawing concern is persuasive under an institutionalist approach: if upstream crude production “relates to” federal officer direction simply because avgas procurement once depended on it, § 1442 would swallow large swaths of state tort litigation without a clear congressional command. Even crediting the Fifth Circuit’s more permissive framing in Latiolais (as Justice Gorsuch notes), the complaint here targets decades of dredging, disposal, and extraction practices not plausibly performed to assist a federal superior in carrying out a delegated wartime task, so the asserted relation is too attenuated to be workable. No colleague identified precedent that would justify collapsing the distinct limits in the statute’s text (“acting under” and “for or relating to”), so my view that removal is improper on this record holds.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains the 2011 amendment adding “or relating to,” but as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, liberal construction is “not limitless,” and the text still requires that the defendant be “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit be tied to an “act under color” of that office. Watson’s delegation/assistance requirement is a meaningful threshold that is not satisfied by mere participation in a wartime-influenced supply chain, and Justice Gorsuch’s concern about an unbounded but-for theory highlights the absence of a workable limiting principle in petitioners’ crude-to-avgas chain. Even assuming some WWII contracts might qualify as “acting under,” these complaints target decades of independent dredging, disposal, and extraction practices not plausibly undertaken to help carry out a federal duty, so the necessary relationship between the claims and federally directed acts is missing. No colleague identified a precedent that would justify collapsing those textual limits into a generalized “upstream input” nexus, so my view remains that removal is improper on this record.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Petitioners’ strongest point—Congress’s 2011 addition of “or relating to,” coupled with the directive to construe § 1442 liberally—still cannot overcome Watson’s threshold requirement that a private entity be “acting under” a federal officer by assisting with a delegated federal task. Chief Justice Roberts’s line-drawing concern is persuasive under a pragmatic, administrable approach: accepting an upstream “crude-to-avgas” but-for chain would make removal turn on remote historical procurement relationships and effectively federalize ordinary state tort suits. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, the complaints target canal dredging, waste disposal, and extraction practices over decades, not the performance of any federally directed wartime obligations, so the necessary concrete connection to the challenged conduct is missing. No colleague has identified a precedent that would justify collapsing these statutory limits into an unbounded nexus theory, so I remain with Respondent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) is to be “liberally construed,” but it is “not limitless,” and Watson v. Philip Morris requires that the defendant be “acting under” federal direction in a way that involves assisting or carrying out a federal officer’s delegated task, not merely operating in a war-influenced or regulated industry. Even accounting for the 2011 amendment adding removal for actions “for or relating to” acts under color of office, that language expands the required nexus only to suits that “stand in some relation” to the federally directed acts; it does not authorize removal based on an attenuated but-for chain from WWII refining/supply contracts to decades of alleged marsh-damaging extraction and disposal practices. Because the parishes’ complaints target conduct largely independent of the federal contracts and do not seek to impose liability for the performance of the federally directed wartime tasks themselves, allowing removal here would unduly federalize state tort law and risk undermining institutional legitimacy by stretching § 1442 beyond its settled limits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) authorizes removal only when the defendant is “acting under” a federal officer and the suit is “for or relating to” an act under color of that office; the 2011 amendment broadened the nexus requirement, but it did not alter the distinct threshold that the private party must be assisting with a federal duty rather than merely operating in an important or regulated industry. Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., 551 U.S. 142 (2007), makes clear that participation in a regulated market (or a wartime-influenced market) is not enough—there must be a delegation-like relationship in which the private actor helps carry out the federal officer’s tasks. Here, the parishes’ claims target long-term coastal-damage conduct (canal dredging, extraction practices, waste disposal) not directed by federal officers, and petitioners’ but-for “crude-to-avgas” theory would stretch “relating to” beyond its ordinary meaning into an effectively unlimited historical chain, collapsing the statute’s limits. Consistent with the statute’s text and Watson’s understanding of “acting under,” removal is improper because the action is not sufficiently connected to any federally directed act that the complaints actually charge.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1), even as amended in 2011 to cover suits “for or relating to any act under color of [federal] office,” still requires a meaningful nexus between the plaintiff’s claims and the defendant’s federally directed conduct; “relating to” cannot be read as an unlimited but-for chain that would federalize ordinary state tort suits whenever a defendant can identify some historic federal contract. Under Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., 551 U.S. 142 (2007), private parties act “under” a federal officer only when they are assisting or carrying out a delegated federal task, not merely operating in an industry affected by wartime coordination or regulation, and the parishes’ complaints target marsh-damaging extraction and disposal practices rather than performance of WWII refining/supply obligations. Petitioners’ theory—treating crude production and downstream environmental impacts as removable because crude was an “indispensable component” of avgas refining—stretches the statutory text beyond its practical limits and would invite a sweeping expansion of federal jurisdiction inconsistent with the statute’s function as a protective, not all-purpose, removal mechanism. On this record, the alleged coastal injuries are too attenuated from any specific “act under color of” federal office to satisfy § 1442(a)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant be “acting under” a federal officer and that the plaintiff’s claims be “for or relating to” an act under color of that office, but Watson v. Philip Morris makes clear that removal does not lie where a private party is merely operating in a federally influenced or regulated market rather than assisting with a delegated federal task. The parishes’ suits target decades of coastal damage from extraction, disposal, and canal dredging—conduct not shown to be directed by federal officers through the WWII refining/supply contracts—so the necessary nexus cannot be satisfied by an unlimited but-for chain tying any upstream crude activity to wartime avgas procurement. The 2011 amendment broadening removal to actions “for or relating to” a federal act may relax the causal-connection requirement, but it did not alter the statute’s threshold “acting under” constraint or erase the need for a concrete connection between the complained-of conduct and the federal direction. Allowing removal on these facts would federalize vast swaths of state tort law based on remote historical contracting, undermining state remedies for communities suffering ongoing environmental harms.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires both that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit is “for or relating to” an act taken under color of federal office; Watson v. Philip Morris makes clear that “acting under” entails assisting with a federal superior’s delegated task, not merely operating in a federally influenced industry. Even crediting that some wartime refining/supply contracts involved qualifying federal direction, these complaints target decades of coastal-damage tortious conduct (canal dredging, waste disposal, extraction practices) that is not plausibly tied to the performance of those specific federal duties, and petitioners’ reliance on an attenuated but-for chain would turn “relating to” (added in 2011) into an atextual, unbounded hook that would federalize vast swaths of state tort law. Read coherently, the 2011 “or relating to” amendment can loosen the nexus requirement at the margins, but it does not dispense with a concrete connection between the charged conduct and the federally directed acts, especially where—on this record—the alleged injuries would have occurred irrespective of the WWII contracts. A narrower construction best fits § 1442’s purpose (protecting federal operations without swallowing state adjudicatory authority) and provides a workable limiting principle consistent with Watson’s core constraint.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) as amended allows removal of actions “for or relating to any act under color of [federal] office,” but the text still requires a meaningful connection between the plaintiff’s claims and the defendant’s federally directed acts; “relating to” cannot be read to authorize removal on an unlimited but-for chain that would federalize ordinary state tort suits whenever a defendant once supplied the Government. Watson v. Philip Morris confirms that a private party “acting under” a federal officer must be assisting with a delegated federal task, not merely operating in an industry influenced by federal policy, and here the parishes’ claims target decades of coastal-damage conduct (canals, disposal, extraction practices) not directed by federal officers under the WWII refining/supply contracts. Even accepting Latiolais’s recognition that “relating to” broadens the nexus, it still demands an association between the complained-of conduct and the federal direction—something more direct than “crude oil is an input to avgas” and thus all upstream coastal operations become removable. Reading the statute to permit removal on that attenuated basis would disregard its limiting words and upset the federal-state balance without a clear congressional command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires both that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the civil action is “for or relating to” an act under color of federal office; the 2011 addition of “relating to” broadened the nexus requirement but did not alter Watson’s core limitation that mere participation in an industry affected by federal policy or contracting is not enough without delegation and direction tied to the conduct being sued upon. Here, the parishes’ coastal-damage claims target decades of extraction, waste disposal, and canal dredging practices, not performance of discrete WWII refining/supply contracts, and petitioners’ but-for chain (crude as an “indispensable component” of wartime refining) risks collapsing the statute into an all-purpose removal device whenever a defendant can identify some historical federal contract. Reading “relating to” to permit removal on such attenuated factual intertwinement would undermine workable limits and upset the federal-state balance in ordinary tort litigation, contrary to the statute’s structure and this Court’s insistence in Watson that “acting under” is broad but “not limitless.” The Fifth Circuit’s narrower approach better preserves the statute’s intended function—protecting federal operations and federal defenses—without federalizing vast swaths of state tort law on a remote wartime-contract theory.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the civil action is “for or relating to” an act under color of federal office; Watson v. Philip Morris limits “acting under” to situations where the private party assists or helps carry out a federal superior’s delegated task, not merely operates in an industry affected by federal influence. Even assuming the WWII refining/supply contracts qualify as “acting under,” these coastal-damage tort suits target decades of dredging, waste disposal, and extraction practices, not performance of those wartime contracts, and petitioners’ proposed but-for chain (“crude is indispensable to refining, so upstream extraction relates to avgas contracts”) is too attenuated to preserve the statute’s textual limits. The 2011 amendment adding “or relating to” broadens the required nexus, but it does not eliminate the need for a genuine connection between the complained-of conduct and the federally directed acts; reading it to cover any historically adjacent private conduct would effectively federalize state tort law whenever a defendant can identify some past federal contracting. Because the parishes’ claims are not sufficiently connected to any federally directed wartime act under color of office, removal is improper.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit is “for or relating to” acts done under color of that office, but Watson v. Philip Morris makes clear that “acting under” demands more than operating in a federally influenced or regulated sector—it requires assisting a federal superior in carrying out delegated tasks under substantial guidance or control. Even crediting that some wartime refining/supply contracts may satisfy “acting under,” the parishes’ tort claims target decades of coastal-damage conduct (canal dredging, waste disposal, extraction practices) not plausibly tied to any specific federally directed wartime performance, and petitioners’ own presentation trends toward an unbounded but-for theory (“crude is indispensable”) that would federalize broad swaths of state tort law whenever a historic federal contract exists. The 2011 amendment’s addition of “or relating to” broadens nexus, but it does not eliminate the requirement of a meaningful connection between the challenged conduct and the federally directed acts; stretching “relating to” to cover generalized upstream production because it was an “indispensable component” of war production is inconsistent with Watson’s limiting principle and with procedural fairness concerns inherent in removal jurisdiction.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether oil companies may remove Louisiana coastal-damage lawsuits to federal court under the federal-officer removal statute based on their WWII-era federal aviation-gasoline procurement/refining contracts—i.e., whether the parishes' claims are sufficiently 'for or relating to' acts performed 'under' a federal officer.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1442(a)(1) (federal-officer removal statute), including the post-2011 language allowing removal for claims 'for or relating to any act under color of such office.'
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Chevron et al.) argue that removal is proper because, during World War II, they performed critical petroleum production/refining work pursuant to federal direction and contracts (often described in terms of PAW wartime mobilization), meaning they were 'acting under' federal officers and the parishes' coastal-land-loss and pollution claims 'relate to' those federally directed activities. They press an expansive reading of 'relating to'—essentially a but-for or broad connection standard—contending there is a straight-line causal relationship between wartime federal fuel requirements and the upstream extraction, handling, and disposal practices the parishes challenge, and that § 1442 is meant to secure a federal forum to prevent state-court interference with federal operations and contractors assisting the government.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Plaquemines and Cameron Parishes and Louisiana) argue that § 1442 does not apply because the complaints target decades of oilfield and canal/dredging and waste-disposal conduct undertaken for commercial purposes and/or under state and private initiatives, not conduct directed by a federal officer under specific federal control. Even if some defendants had WWII refining contracts, respondents contend the suit is not 'for' those refining activities and is not sufficiently 'relating to' them: the challenged marsh-damaging conduct would have occurred irrespective of avgas contracts (so petitioners cannot satisfy even a but-for theory on these pleadings/record), and Watson-style limits on 'acting under' prevent transforming ordinary, heavily regulated or federally contracting industry activity into automatic federal-officer removal for any later state-law tort suit with a remote historical connection.
key_precedents: Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., 551 U.S. 142 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is that the 2011 addition of “for or relating to” broadened the nexus requirement, potentially allowing some looser connection than strict causation. But as Justice Kavanaugh underscores, that amendment does not displace Watson’s separate threshold that the defendant was actually “acting under” federal “subjection, guidance, or control” with respect to the conduct the suit targets, and accepting an attenuated WWII-procurement narrative would risk turning § 1442 into a near-general contractor removal provision. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces my minimalist approach: we can affirm narrowly on this record because defendants have not concretely linked the specific canal/dredging/disposal practices alleged to be wrongful to any federally directed acts taken under color of office. No colleague has identified a precedent that would justify collapsing “acting under” and “under color” into a but-for “relating to” test, so a limited affirmance best preserves the statute’s structure and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ best textual point is that Congress in 2011 broadened § 1442(a)(1) by adding “or relating to,” but that amendment cannot erase the statute’s separate, antecedent requirement that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer with “subjection, guidance, or control” over the conduct at issue, as Watson holds. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrability concern is persuasive on originalist grounds: reading “relating to” as a mere historical but-for hook would effectively sever “acting under” and “under color of such office” from any real work and convert the provision into a general contractor-removal statute—something the enacted text does not say. Even if discrete WWII avgas procurement involved close federal direction, the pleaded wrongs here concern decades of canal dredging, extraction, and disposal undertaken for private commercial ends, with no concrete showing that those specific acts were performed under federal direction. No colleague identified any precedent that justifies collapsing these distinct textual requirements into an unbounded nexus test, so removal remains improper on this record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains the 2011 amendment adding “or relating to,” which they say relaxes the causal-nexus requirement enough to capture a historical chain from WWII avgas procurement to later coastal harms. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh stress, that broader nexus cannot erase Watson’s threshold requirement that defendants were actually “acting under” federal “subjection, guidance, or control” in performing the conduct the suit targets; on this record, the pleaded wrongs are decades of canal-dredging, extraction, and disposal practices undertaken for commercial ends, not federally directed acts. Accepting a but-for “relating to” theory would, as Justice Gorsuch notes, collapse the statute’s distinct “acting under” and “under color of office” limits and create an effectively unbounded contractor-removal rule with serious federalism and administrability consequences. No colleague identified a precedent undermining Watson’s limiting principle or showing that remote procurement history alone suffices, so removal remains improper.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point remains that Congress’s 2011 addition of “for or relating to” loosened the causal-nexus showing, but that cannot bypass Watson’s threshold requirement that the defendant was actually “acting under” federal “subjection, guidance, or control” with respect to the conduct the plaintiff is suing about. As Justice Kagan explains, accepting a purely historical but-for “relating to” theory would make § 1442 a broad contractor-removal device, undermining federalism and denying local communities a state forum for long-term environmental harms. Even if discrete WWII avgas work could qualify, the record does not concretely link the parishes’ pleaded canal/dredging, extraction, and disposal practices to federally directed acts “under color of office,” so the asserted nexus is too remote to justify removal. No colleague identified precedent that collapses “acting under” and “under color” into an unbounded nexus test, so my pragmatic view remains that removal must stay tethered to the specific wrongful conduct alleged.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that Congress’s 2011 addition of “or relating to” loosened the nexus beyond strict causation, so a nontrivial connection to wartime avgas procurement could in theory support removal. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, that broader nexus cannot erase Watson’s separate threshold that the defendant was actually “acting under” federal subjection, guidance, or control with respect to the conduct the suit targets; otherwise “relating to” becomes an unadministrable but-for test that effectively converts § 1442 into a general contractor-removal statute. On this record, the complaints are aimed at decades of canal/dredging, extraction, and disposal practices undertaken for defendants’ commercial ends, and petitioners have not concretely tethered those alleged wrongs to federally directed acts taken under color of office. Under a pragmatic textualist approach, reading the statute to require a meaningful, conduct-specific linkage best preserves statutory coherence and workable limiting principles without denying removal where genuine federal delegation is shown.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioners’ best point is the 2011 amendment adding “for or relating to,” which Justice Kavanaugh notes relaxes the old causal-nexus requirement; but that broader nexus cannot erase Watson’s separate threshold that the defendant was actually “acting under” federal “subjection, guidance, or control” in performing the conduct the suit targets. Chief Justice Roberts’s administrable limiting principle is persuasive: if a remote wartime procurement relationship suffices to remove decades-later state tort claims centered on canals, dredging, and disposal, § 1442 becomes a near-general contractor removal statute—something the text’s “acting under” and “under color of office” language does not clearly authorize. Even accepting that discrete WWII avgas refining might qualify as “acting under,” the complaints here do not meaningfully tether the alleged wrongful acts to federally directed performance, so “relating to” cannot be stretched into a mere but-for historical connection without collapsing the statute’s distinct requirements. No colleague identified a precedent that justifies that collapse, so my position stands.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point is that the 2011 amendment’s addition of “or relating to” relaxed the causal-nexus requirement, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that this cannot be read to erase Watson’s independent threshold: the defendant must be genuinely “acting under” federal subjection, guidance, or control with respect to the conduct the suit targets. Even if discrete WWII avgas procurement work involved close federal direction, the parishes’ complaints principally challenge decades of canal-dredging, extraction, and waste-disposal practices undertaken for commercial operations, and the asserted wartime relationship is too attenuated to be “under color” of federal office in any administrable way. Justice Gorsuch’s warning about an unbounded but-for theory is persuasive to me as a practical and institutional matter: accepting that theory would risk converting § 1442 into a general contractor-removal statute without a clear congressional command. No colleague has identified a precedent that compels collapsing the statute’s separate “acting under” and “under color” requirements into a broad historical-connection test on this record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioners’ best point remains that Congress’s 2011 insertion of “or relating to” in § 1442(a)(1) loosened the nexus requirement, potentially reaching beyond strict causation. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the text still imposes two distinct constraints: the defendant must be “acting under” a federal officer (as limited by Watson’s “subjection, guidance, or control”), and the suit must be “for or relating to” acts taken “under color” of that office. Even assuming discrete WWII avgas work could satisfy “acting under,” the complaints here target decades of canal-dredging, extraction, and disposal practices not shown on this record to be federally directed, making the asserted “relating to” connection too attenuated and effectively a but-for theory that would collapse the statute’s separate textual elements. No colleague identified a precedent that would justify reading “relating to” to override Watson’s threshold or to untether removal from the conduct actually alleged to be wrongful.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point remains that Congress’s 2011 addition of “for or relating to” broadened the nexus, potentially allowing a looser connection between WWII avgas procurement and later extraction activities. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan both stress, that broader nexus does not erase Watson’s separate “acting under” threshold—subjection, guidance, or control in carrying out the conduct the suit targets—and reading “relating to” as mere historical but-for linkage would collapse the statute’s distinct requirements and produce the unadministrable, effectively unbounded removal rule Justice Alito warns against. Even assuming discrete wartime refining could qualify as “acting under,” the complaints principally challenge decades of canal/dredging/disposal and field practices, and on this record defendants have not concretely tied those alleged wrongs to federally directed acts taken under color of office. Procedural fairness and practical consequences favor an evidence-tethered rule: absent a specific linkage between the pleaded harmful conduct and federal direction, state-law remediation claims should remain in state court.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer—i.e., subject to the officer’s “subjection, guidance, or control” and assisting in carrying out federal duties—and that the suit is “for or relating to” acts taken under color of that office. Watson v. Philip Morris cautions that ordinary commercial activity (even if heavily regulated or involving federal dealings) does not satisfy “acting under” absent the kind of close federal direction that makes the private party an agent in executing federal tasks. On this record, the parishes’ coastal-damage claims principally target decades of extraction, canal/dredging, and waste-disposal practices, and the asserted WWII avgas procurement/refining contracts are at most a remote historical backdrop rather than a sufficiently tight nexus to the challenged conduct, so removal would risk an unduly expansive construction that would sweep vast categories of state tort suits into federal court. A narrow disposition affirming remand best respects precedent and the statute’s limiting principles while avoiding a broad jurisdictional rule with significant institutional and federalism consequences.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 28 U.S.C. § 1442(a)(1) permits removal only when a defendant is sued “for or relating to” acts taken “under color” of a federal officer, which presupposes the defendant was actually “acting under” federal direction in performing the conduct the complaint targets. Under Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., “acting under” requires assisting federal officers in carrying out federal duties with “subjection, guidance, or control,” not merely operating in an industry that at some point contracted with or was regulated by the Federal Government. Here, the parishes’ claims focus on long-running coastal and pollution harms from extraction, canal/dredging, and disposal practices undertaken for commercial oil production, not the discrete WWII avgas procurement/refining work allegedly directed by federal officers. Even crediting the 2011 amendment’s broader “relating to” language, the required link must be to federally directed acts, and a remote historical connection to wartime refining contracts is insufficient to transform these state-law tort suits into federal-officer cases.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the suit is “for or relating to” acts under color of that office; the 2011 amendment broadens the nexus requirement but does not erase the separate “acting under” and meaningful-connection limits. Under Watson v. Philip Morris, a private party “acts under” only when it is assisting the Government in carrying out federal duties with subjection, guidance, or control, not merely doing ordinary commercial work that happens to be regulated or historically connected to wartime procurement. These parishes’ complaints target decades of coastal-damage conduct (canals, dredging, disposal, extraction practices) undertaken for commercial production and state/private initiatives, and the asserted WWII avgas refining contracts are at most a remote historical backdrop rather than the specific conduct sued upon. Adopting petitioners’ essentially but-for “relating to” theory here would create an unbounded removal rule for major industries with any federal contracting history, a practical consequence § 1442’s text and Watson’s limiting principle do not support.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) is a protective jurisdictional statute, but it still requires that the defendant be “acting under” a federal officer in the Watson sense—i.e., assisting a federal superior with tasks the Government otherwise would perform, under “subjection, guidance, or control,” not merely operating in a regulated industry or having some federal contracts. The 2011 addition of “for or relating to” broadened the required connection, but it did not eliminate Watson’s threshold “acting under” limitation, nor does it permit removal where the pleaded claims target decades of commercial extraction, canal/dredging, and waste-disposal practices not directed by federal officers. On this record, the asserted WWII avgas procurement/refining contracts are at most a remote historical backdrop, not a sufficiently direct relationship between the parishes’ coastal-damage claims and specific federally controlled conduct to justify depriving Louisiana communities of their chosen state forum. Allowing removal on so attenuated a link would convert § 1442 into an overbroad escape hatch for powerful defendants and would undermine fairness and access to justice for vulnerable coastal parishes seeking remediation under state law.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) still requires that defendants both be “acting under” a federal officer and show the suit is “for or relating to” acts taken “under color” of that office; the 2011 addition of “or relating to” broadens the nexus inquiry but does not erase Watson’s limit that ordinary commercial activity (even if federally regulated or incidentally connected to federal procurement) is not enough without governmental direction and control. Here the parishes’ complaints target decades of canal-dredging, extraction, and waste-disposal practices undertaken for defendants’ own commercial operations, not specific federally directed avgas-refining performance, and the asserted WWII contracts are too remote to supply a workable, non-boundless “relating to” connection. Reading “relating to” as essentially any historical but-for link would turn § 1442 into a general contractor-removal statute for later state-law tort suits, contrary to the statute’s structure and Watson’s “not limitless” admonition. On this record, petitioners have not shown the necessary nexus between the challenged conduct and any acts performed under federal officers, so removal is improper.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) permits removal only when the suit is “for or relating to any act under color of” federal office and the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer, meaning it was assisting the Government in carrying out federal duties under “subjection, guidance, or control,” not merely operating in a federally influenced marketplace. Watson v. Philip Morris draws the limiting principle: ordinary regulation—or historically adjacent contracting untethered to the alleged wrongs—does not transform later state-law tort claims into federal-officer cases. Even accepting that WWII aviation-gasoline contracts could qualify as “acting under” for discrete refining work, these complaints target decades of coastal-damage conduct (canals, dredging, waste disposal) not shown on this record to be directed by federal officers or sufficiently connected to the contract performance beyond a remote “straight-line” narrative. Reading “relating to” to reach any but-for historical connection would expand § 1442 beyond its text and purpose into a general contractor-removal statute, upsetting federal-state jurisdictional lines without a clear congressional command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) as amended in 2011 allows removal for claims “for or relating to” acts under color of federal office, which broadens the nexus requirement, but it does not eliminate Watson’s threshold requirement that the defendant was truly “acting under” a federal officer through delegation and close direction, not merely operating in a regulated industry or under general procurement relationships. On these pleadings and record, the parishes’ coastal-damage claims target decades of extraction, canal/dredging, and waste-disposal practices undertaken for commercial operations, and the asserted WWII avgas refining/procurement contracts are too attenuated to make the suit one “for or relating to” federally directed acts in any workable, limiting-principle sense. Reading “relating to” as essentially unlimited but-for connection—especially where the same upstream conduct would have occurred absent the wartime contracts—would risk converting ordinary state-law tort suits into routine federal-officer removals, contrary to Watson’s limiting framework and to the Court’s institutional interest in a principled, administrable rule. The proper course is to require a concrete linkage between the specific federally directed performance and the conduct alleged to be wrongful, which respondents say is missing here.

Under Watson v. Philip Morris Cos., 551 U.S. 142 (2007), private parties qualify only when they assist federal officers in carrying out governmental duties under subjection, guidance, or control—not merely because they operated in a federally influenced market or performed ordinary commercial activity that incidentally supported federal needs. Even assuming certain WWII avgas/refining contracts involved adequate federal direction for the refining work, the parishes’ complaints target decades of coastal land-loss conduct (canals, dredging, waste disposal, and field practices) not shown on this record to be acts performed under federal control, and the asserted “relating to” link is too remote to tie these state-law claims to the specific federally directed contractual performance contemplated by § 1442(a)(1). Respecting text and precedent, removal cannot rest on a generalized historical connection between wartime procurement and the upstream extraction/land-management practices the parishes challenge.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1442(a)(1) requires that the defendant was “acting under” a federal officer and that the plaintiff’s claims are “for or relating to” acts done under color of that office; the 2011 addition of “relating to” relaxes the nexus requirement but does not erase the threshold “acting under” limits. Under Watson v. Philip Morris, “acting under” demands more than participation in a regulated industry or generalized wartime contracting—it requires subjection, guidance, or control in a way that helps federal officers carry out governmental duties. Here, the parishes’ complaints target decades of coastal-land-loss and pollution-causing extraction/canal/dredging/disposal practices, and petitioners’ WWII avgas procurement/refining contracts do not, on this record, supply a sufficiently direct connection between federally directed conduct and the specific marsh-damaging acts alleged. Allowing removal on this attenuated historical link would expand § 1442 beyond its practical purpose and undermine procedural fairness by forcing state-law tort claims into federal court without a concrete showing that the suit is actually about federally controlled conduct.
